He was a member thereof. The assessee, who was a member, was a member. The assessee received a sum of Rs. 36,396/8/ to Babu Har Narain Singh and his heirs. The assessee claimed that the allowance was in fact a payment of the compensation for relinquishing the title to those lands. The Income tax Officer held that the allowance had been made in the nature of a revenue receipt and not taxable. The High Court held that the assessee was not liable to pay the compensation for the extinguishment of the right to sue. Held, that the allowance made by the assessee was a payment of money and not a payment of compensation for relinquishes the title to the lands in dispute. The allowance was not a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title to the land in dispute. It was a payment in cash or in kind. The allowance made by an assessee was not taxable as income. The allowance, though it was a payment made in cash or kind, was not taxable. In the absence of any evidence to show that the allowance or payment was a payment, the allowance was not taxable, and the allowance was a payment. The allowance is revenue income. The High court was right in holding that the allowance did not amount to a payment of income. The payment of the allowance was revenue income. In the present case the allowance was made in kind. In the circumstances of the case the allowance made was not taxable in the hands of the assessee. The allowance did not in fact amount a payment of a revenue nature. The allowance had been rightly made in the present case. The allowance could not be regarded as a payment of revenue. The allowance in question was not taxable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The amount paid to the assessee is revenue income and not exempt from taxation. The allowance has to be regarded as the capital receipt. In the case of a capital receipt the allowance is not taxable.
